content: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic used to treat a wide range of bacterial infections. It can also be prescribed to prevent certain bacterial infections. However, it is only effective against bacterial infections and will not work for viral infections such as the common cold or flu. This medication should be taken orally as directed by your doctor, typically before a meal. It is best absorbed on an empty stomach. Do not crush the medication, as it has a bitter taste; instead, swallow it whole. The dosage and duration of treatment depend on your medical condition and response to therapy. For optimal results, take this antibiotic at evenly spaced intervals. If you are using it to treat an infection, continue taking it for the full prescribed duration, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Stopping the medication too early may cause the infection to return. If you are taking it to prevent infections, follow your doctor’s instructions precisely. Common side effects may include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain or cramping, and loss of appetite. Taking the medication with food may help reduce these symptoms. Remember, this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Rarely, erythromycin may cause a severe intestinal condition due to a bacteria called Clostridium difficile (C. difficile), which can occur during treatment or weeks to months after stopping the medication. Prolonged or repeated use of this medication may lead to oral thrush or a new yeast infection. Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare but possible. Before taking erythromycin, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, other macrolide antibiotics (such as azithromycin or clarithromycin), or any other substances. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Erythromycin may also cause a condition affecting the heart rhythm known as QT prolongation, which can increase the risk of serious irregular heartbeats. The risk of QT prolongation may be higher if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low potassium or magnesium levels in the blood can also increase this risk, especially if caused by severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting, or if you are taking diuretics (water pills). Erythromycin may interfere with the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. Some erythromycin products may contain sodium, and the medication can pass into breast milk. Drug interactions may alter how erythromycin or other medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Erythromycin can slow the removal of certain drugs from your body, potentially affecting their effectiveness. If someone overdoses and experiences severe symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. This medication should only be used for your current condition and not shared with others. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is near the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store erythromycin at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed, following local disposal guidelines. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about this product. It does not guarantee that the medication is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
